property_summary: For all callers and amounts, only the Owner can successfully withdraw the entire contract balance via withdraw(); the mutant that removes the require will allow some non-owners to successfully withdraw (changing address(c).balance to zero when called by a non-owner).

For every caller and any prior balance, only the Owner can successfully cause the contract balance to become zero by calling withdraw(); the mutant (which removes the Owner check) allows some non-Owner caller to empty the contract, violating that property.

For every caller address and any initial contract balance, in the reference C only the Owner can transfer the contract balance out via withdraw() (calls by non-Owner do not change address(c).balance), whereas the mutant that removes the Owner check allows some non-Owner caller to succeed and thus can change address(c).balance to zero for some inputs; we encode this by fuzzing a caller and initial funded amount and asserting that if the caller is not Owner then a withdraw call does not reduce address(c).balance (i.e., balance remains unchanged).

For every caller and any initial contract balance, in the reference C a withdraw() call reverts for non-Owner callers (so it cannot succeed and cannot transfer funds out), but the mutant (removing the require) allows some non-Owner caller to successfully withdraw; we assert that non-Owner withdraw attempts always revert (ok==false) for all fuzzed caller addresses and amounts.

For every caller and any initial contract balance, if the caller is not Owner then calling withdraw() does not change address(c).balance (i.e., only Owner can successfully reduce the contract balance to zero); the mutant removing the Owner require allows some non-Owner caller to reduce the balance, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the Owner, calling withdraw() transfers the contract's entire balance to the Owner address (so address(c).balance becomes 0 and Owner's balance increases accordingly); the mutant sends funds to msg.sender instead, causing Owner to not receive the contract balance for some inputs.

For any caller who is the contract Owner, calling withdraw() sends the entire contract balance to the stored Owner address (so after withdraw address(c).balance == 0 and Owner's balance increases if Owner is msg.sender); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender instead will cause the stored Owner not to receive the contract balance for some callers, breaking the rule that Owner is the recipient of the contract balance when Owner calls withdraw().

For any caller who is the stored Owner and after funding the contract, calling withdraw() always transfers the contract's entire balance to the stored Owner (so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can leave the contract balance nonzero when the caller is not the stored Owner, breaking this rule for some fuzzed caller addresses.

For every caller who is the stored Owner and any contract balance > 0, after Owner calls withdraw() the contract balance becomes zero (the entire balance is transferred to Owner); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender instead can leave the contract with nonzero balance when Owner is not msg.sender (i.e., when msg.sender != Owner) — but since withdraw requires sender==Owner, the real distinction is that the correct contract sends funds to the stored Owner, while the mutant sends to msg.sender; thus the rule: if withdraw is invoked by the stored Owner, address(c).balance == 0 afterwards — the mutant will violate this for some fuzzed inputs because it sends funds to msg.sender rather than the stored Owner.

For any caller that equals the stored Owner and any positive contract balance funded by that Owner, after Owner calls withdraw() the contract balance becomes zero (the Owner receives the entire balance); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can leave the contract balance nonzero for some fuzzed funding amounts and caller addresses (violating this rule).

Reference contract: only the Owner can successfully call withdraw (calls by Owner always transfer the contract balance and do not revert); the mutant inverts the require so Owner calls to withdraw are rejected—violating that rule.
For every caller, when the contract Owner calls withdraw the call succeeds and transfers out the contract balance; the mutant inverts the require so Owner calls will revert (fail) for some inputs.

For every admissible input, if the contract Owner calls withdraw (sending any amount of gas/value), the call succeeds and the contract's balance becomes zero; the mutant inverts the require and thus can make an Owner withdraw call fail (or not transfer out the balance) for some inputs.

For any fuzzed caller address, when the contract Owner calls withdraw the call succeeds (does not revert) and therefore returns normally; the mutant inverts the require and causes Owner calls to revert for some inputs.

For every caller address provided, when the contract Owner calls withdraw (i.e. msg.sender == Owner) the call always succeeds (does not revert) and thus returns normally; the mutant inverts the require so Owner calls can revert, breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any caller Owner and any balance held by the contract, after Owner calls withdraw() the contract balance becomes zero (the reference always forwards the full balance to Owner); the mutant that sends only half can leave a non-zero contract balance for some inputs.

For any caller who is Owner, after calling withdraw() the contract balance becomes zero (the reference always drains the full balance to Owner); the mutant that sends only half can leave a non-zero contract balance for some initial balances and so violates this rule.

For any Owner caller and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw() transfers the entire contract balance to Owner (so address(c).balance becomes zero); the mutant that sends only half can leave a nonzero contract balance for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller equal to Owner and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw() forwards the entire contract balance to Owner (so Owner's balance increases by exactly the contract balance and address(c).balance becomes zero); the mutant that sends only half will make Owner's balance increase by less than the prior contract balance for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For any caller equal to Owner and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw() transfers the entire contract balance out of C (so address(c).balance becomes zero); the mutant that sends only half can leave a nonzero contract balance for some fuzzed deposit amounts and thus violates this rule.

For all callers and balances, when Owner (the deployer) calls withdraw(), the contract's entire balance is transferred out so address(c).balance becomes zero; the mutant that uses Owner.call and ignores success can leave funds in the contract when the recipient fails, breaking this property for some inputs (failing recipient).

For any caller and any ether value, when the Owner invokes withdraw() the reference always makes the contract balance become zero (all funds are transferred out); the mutant using Owner.call and ignoring the call success can leave funds trapped when the Owner's fallback reverts, violating this property for some inputs.

For any caller and calldata, when the Owner calls Command forwarding some ETH, the reference contract forwards the same msg.value to the callee (so the callee can receive the value) whereas the mutant uses staticcall (no value) causing the callee to receive zero and thus behavior diverges for callees that require or observe nonzero value.

For any caller and calldata, only the Owner can execute Command and such execution does not modify C's storage (notably it does not change the public Owner getter); the delegatecall mutant can execute code in C's context and may change storage (e.g., Owner), breaking this invariant for some calldata/target.

For every admissible Command invocation by Owner, after Command returns the contract's public Owner address remains equal to the original deployer (the reference preserves Owner), but the delegatecall mutant can change storage and thus can make Owner differ for some calldata/target.

For any calldata and target provided by the owner, the reference contract's storage (specifically the public Owner) and balance-transfer behavior are preserved after Command: calling Command never changes Owner or drains contract balance unless the target is the contract itself invoking payable logic; the delegatecall mutant can execute code that mutates storage (e.g. change Owner) or otherwise alter observable state — so there exists calldata and a malicious target contract that, when delegatecalled, changes Owner, violating this invariant.

For every admissible inputs, when the Owner calls Command the reference C does not have its storage mutated by the callee (notably Owner remains the deployer); the delegatecall mutant can run target code in C's context and mutate storage (e.g. change Owner), violating this rule for some calldata/target.

After any call to Command invoked by the Owner, the contract's Owner remains equal to the caller (msg.sender) in the reference implementation, but the mutant clears Owner to address(0) after the call which violates this invariant for some inputs (when Owner calls Command).

For every admissible input where the current Owner calls Command on c, the contract's public Owner remains equal to that caller after Command returns (reference preserves Owner), but the mutant that clears Owner after the call breaks this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and calldata, if a non-owner address calls Command (i.e., msg.sender != Owner) the reference C leaves Owner unchanged and does not clear it; the mutant that unconditionally sets Owner = address(0) after the call would change Owner when a non-owner successfully calls Command (which should be disallowed by require), so instead we assert that only the Owner can call Command (the call succeeds only when msg.sender == Owner) — the reference enforces this for all admissible inputs while the mutant still enforces it, but we need a property that distinguishes them: if Owner calls Command that executes a failing external call (reverting callee), the reference will keep Owner equal to the caller even if the callee reverts (because the require ensures only Owner can call and the call revert will revert the whole Command, leaving state unchanged), whereas the mutant would also revert before clearing Owner; to detect the mutant we instead use an attacker that performs a successful low-level call (returns false but does not revert) — the reference preserves Owner after a successful external call while the mutant clears Owner after the call completes, so the rule is: when the current Owner calls Command and the callee accepts the funds and returns normally (i.e., call does not revert), Owner remains equal to the caller; the mutant breaks this by clearing Owner to address(0) for some inputs.

Calling Command(adr,data) with msg.sender == Owner does not change Owner's ETH balance beyond transferring msg.value to adr (i.e., the contract must not additionally forward msg.value to Owner); the mutant erroneously transfers msg.value to Owner after the call, increasing Owner's balance for some inputs.

For any caller and any msg.value, if msg.value is at least the contract balance before the call, then after calling multiplicate the contract's balance becomes zero (the entire balance plus msg.value is forwarded out); the mutant using '>' violates this when msg.value equals the previous balance, leaving funds in the contract.

For every call to multiplicate when msg.value >= address(c).balance, the contract forwards its entire balance plus msg.value out (leaving c.balance == 0); the mutant changing >= to > fails this rule for inputs where msg.value == address(c).balance.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) the reference contract forwards out its entire balance plus msg.value whenever msg.value >= previous contract balance (so address(c).balance == 0 after the call); the mutant using '>' can leave a nonzero balance when msg.value == previous balance, so the property is violated for those inputs.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) with any caller and any msg.value, if msg.value >= prior address(c).balance then the reference forwards all funds so address(c).balance == 0 after the call; the mutant (using >) violates this when msg.value == prior balance leaving nonzero balance.

For all calls to multiplicate(address) the reference contract ensures that if msg.value == address(c).balance before the call, it will transfer out the sum (leaving c.balance == 0); the mutant (changing >= to >) can leave nonzero balance when msg.value == prior balance, so the rule is: if msg.value >= prior balance then address(c).balance == 0 after the call — we will restrict to admissible inputs to avoid other failures and let the fuzzer find the case msg.value == prior balance that breaks the mutant.

For every call to multiplicate(addr) when the caller sends at least the contract's current balance (msg.value >= address(c).balance), the reference contract always forwards all available funds (contract balance + msg.value) to the target address (so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards); the mutant inverts the condition and therefore can fail to forward in some cases where msg.value >= balance, breaking this property.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) the reference contract forwards all funds (leaving address(c).balance == 0) whenever msg.value >= address(c).balance; the mutant inverting the condition can leave funds in the contract for some fuzzed msg.value and target adr causing address(c).balance != 0.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) with caller sending msg.value >= address(c).balance, the reference contract always forwards all available funds (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant inverting the if-condition can fail to forward in that case, leaving a non-zero contract balance.

For any caller sending value v to multiplicate(adr) when the callee adr's fallback reverts, the reference C will NOT attempt to transfer (so the call to adr fails only if it would have been attempted), while the mutant inverts the condition causing it to attempt (and thus revert) for some v — therefore: for all admissible inputs where adr is a reverting contract, the reference never reverts from multiplicate (call returns ok=true), but the mutant can cause multiplicate to revert (ok=false) for some fuzzed msg.value.

For any caller and any target contract with a payable fallback that ACCEPTS payments, calling multiplicate(adr) with any msg.value never increases c's balance (i.e., address(c).balance after the call is <= before the call) in the reference; the mutant can, for some msg.value and target, leave or increase the contract balance compared to the pre-call balance, breaking this rule.

For any caller and any msg.value, calling multiplicate(adr) on the correct contract never reduces the contract's balance below its pre-call balance (it only transfers out when msg.value >= prior balance), whereas the mutant always transfers address(this).balance + msg.value away unconditionally, which can reduce the contract balance for some inputs (making address(c).balance after the call less than before).
